title: Home Insurance Adjuster Estimate Too Low? What to Do Next
description: Home insurance adjuster estimate too low? Learn why Galveston claims get underpaid, how to read the estimate, and the steps to request a fair supplement.
keyword: home insurance adjuster estimate too low
html:
You finally get the estimate from your insurance company, and the number is nowhere near what contractors are quoting to fix your home. If your home insurance adjuster estimate is too low, you are not stuck with it. An estimate is the insurer's opening evaluation, and it can be questioned, corrected and supplemented with the right documentation.

Seeing a home insurance adjuster estimate too low to cover real repair costs is one of the most common frustrations after a Gulf Coast storm or fire. This guide explains why estimates come in low, how to read one, and the practical steps Galveston homeowners can take to request a fair adjustment on a windstorm, hurricane, fire or water claim.

Why a Home Insurance Adjuster Estimate Is Too Low

Low estimates usually come from a handful of predictable causes, not a single big mistake:

  • Missed damage. A quick inspection may skip the attic, interior ceilings, one elevation of the roof, or detached structures.
  • Incomplete scope. The estimate may include replacing shingles but omit underlayment, drip edge, starter strips, ridge cap, flashing, or removal and disposal.
  • Repair instead of replace. The insurer may price a patch when matching materials are no longer available or the damage is widespread.
  • Pricing that does not reflect local conditions. After a storm, labor and material costs in Galveston County can rise and contractors may be hard to schedule.
  • Heavy depreciation. On replacement cost policies, depreciation withheld up front may be recoverable later, but only if you follow the policy's steps.
  • Code items left out. Rebuilding may require work to meet current code. Whether that is paid depends on your ordinance or law coverage. See our Galveston local code page for common requirements.
  • No overhead and profit. When a project needs a general contractor to coordinate multiple trades, contractor overhead and profit are often a legitimate part of the cost.

How to Read Your Insurance Estimate

Most insurers use estimating software that produces a line-item report. Take it room by room and ask:

  1. Is every damaged area listed? Compare the rooms and elevations in the estimate to your own photos.
  2. Are the quantities right? Check square footage of roofing, drywall, flooring and paint. Small measurement errors multiply quickly.
  3. Is each necessary step included? Tear out, haul away, prep, install, prime, paint, and cleanup should all appear where needed.
  4. How much depreciation was taken, and is it recoverable? Look for a column or summary showing recoverable versus non-recoverable depreciation.
  5. What deductible was applied? Windstorm and hurricane deductibles on the coast are often a percentage of the dwelling limit.

Our claim settlement calculator helps you see how deductible and depreciation affect what you actually receive.

Step-by-Step: What to Do When the Estimate Is Too Low

1. Do not cash the check as a final settlement without reading it

Many initial payments are partial and do not close the claim, but check the check, the cover letter and any release language. If anything suggests full and final settlement, get clarification in writing before you proceed.

2. Get detailed contractor estimates

Ask licensed, reputable contractors for itemized estimates, not one-line totals. An itemized estimate can be compared directly to the insurer's line items.

3. Document what was missed

Take dated photos and video of any damage not in the estimate. Include measurements. For roofs, photograph each slope and any lifted, creased or missing shingles. For interiors, capture water stains, warped flooring and damaged insulation.

4. Send a written supplement request

Write to your adjuster with a clear list of disputed items, the reason each should be included, and supporting photos or contractor estimates. Keep it factual and organized so the reviewer can check each item quickly.

5. Ask for a re-inspection

If the original inspection missed areas, request a re-inspection and be there for it. Bring your contractor or public adjuster if you have one.

6. Track deadlines and responses

Texas insurers must follow the claim-handling deadlines in the Prompt Payment of Claims Act, Chapter 542 of the Insurance Code. Log every communication and ask for written responses. For TWIA windstorm claims, the rules in Chapter 2210 of the Insurance Code apply, and TWIA's letters will explain your dispute options and their deadlines.

Mistakes to Avoid

  • Starting full repairs before documenting everything. Emergency repairs are fine and often required, but photograph conditions first.
  • Arguing in general terms. Saying the number is too low rarely changes anything. Pointing to specific missing line items with photos does.
  • Relying on phone calls. Follow up every call with a short email summarizing what was discussed.
  • Missing depreciation recovery steps. Find out what proof of completed repairs your insurer needs and by when.

A home insurance adjuster estimate too low by a wide margin is often a sign that areas were missed entirely, not just priced differently. Walk the whole property again with the estimate in hand.

Special Considerations for TWIA Estimates

Windstorm claims on Galveston Island are often handled by the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association. TWIA claims must be reported within one year of the date of loss, and TWIA's dispute process has its own structure and time limits. If you believe a TWIA estimate is too low, read every letter you receive carefully and act within the dates it gives. Our TWIA claims expert page covers this in more detail.

If You Still Cannot Agree

When you and the insurer disagree on the amount of loss, options may include:

  • Appraisal, if your policy includes an appraisal clause. Each side names an appraiser, and an umpire resolves differences on amount of loss.
  • A complaint to the Texas Department of Insurance (TDI), which can prompt the insurer to respond to your concerns.
  • Consulting a Texas insurance attorney for coverage disputes or potential bad faith.

How a Public Adjuster Helps With a Low Estimate

When a home insurance adjuster estimate is too low, the fix is usually better documentation and a more complete scope. That is exactly what a public adjuster provides. Licensed by TDI and working for you rather than the insurer, a public adjuster re-inspects the property, writes a detailed competing estimate, and negotiates line by line with the carrier. There is no guarantee of a particular result, but a complete, well-supported claim gives you the best footing.

Underpaid Claim Checklist

  • Full estimate and policy in hand
  • Rooms, quantities and steps compared with your own photos
  • Depreciation and deductible understood
  • Itemized contractor estimates obtained
  • Missed damage documented with dated photos
  • Written supplement request sent
  • Re-inspection requested
  • All deadlines calendared

faq.q: Can I negotiate with my home insurance adjuster?
faq.a: Yes. An insurance estimate is not final just because it was issued. You can submit contractor estimates, photos and a written list of missed items, and request a re-inspection or supplement.

faq.q: Should I cash the insurance check if the estimate is too low?
faq.a: Many initial payments are partial and do not close the claim, but read the check, cover letter and any release language first. If anything suggests the payment is a full and final settlement, get written clarification before depositing it.

On many replacement cost policies, the insurer first pays actual cash value and holds back depreciation. That withheld amount can often be recovered after repairs are completed, as long as you follow the policy's requirements and deadlines.
